title: How did you implement Attribute-based Access Control (ABAC) in Spring Boot?
body_excerpt: I’ve been working on an issue in our Spring Boot application for some time now: authorization . Because we have a more complex permission model — permissions depend not only on roles, but also on user-specific attributes (e.g., department) — we require Attribute-based Access Control (ABAC) instead of the typical Role-based Access Control (RBAC) used in Spring Security (see Spring Docs - Method-based Security ). At the moment, we have a custom implementation that roughly follows the ABAC reference model (PEP, PDP, ...). However, it is neither particularly efficient nor easily scalable or maintainable. Therefore, I’d like to hear what solutions you have used and what has worked well in your projects. Below are some approaches I have explored or tested, but none of them seem to be a perfect fit so far: SpEL (Method-based Security: @PreAuthorize / @PostAuthorize) Spring allows you to define authorization logic directly in annotations using SpEL. However, this is recommended only for simple logic (see Spring Docs - Favor Granting Authorities ). Since our use case is more complex, this approach does not seem suitable. SpEL - Programmatic Authorization Instead of writing logic directly in SpEL, one can reference a separate service from SpEL, which then performs the authorization checks. title: Why does Python get a red carpet to vSphere while Java gets a CAPTCHA and a shrug?
body_excerpt: VMware’s pyVmomi is the velvet-rope VIP pass to vSphere: whisper [code] , and the data center parts like the Red Sea. It’s a universal remote with actual buttons, not stickers. Java, meanwhile, gets an escape room. There is a library—somewhere—guarded by a portal that demands an account, three riddles, two CAPTCHAs, a blood oath to the EULA, and an OTP delivered via carrier pigeon. The REST coverage? Like IKEA furniture missing the bag of screws: “Technically a table if you believe hard enough.” Documentation? Python devs are reading it before their espresso cools. Java devs are spelunking through a SharePoint from the Bronze Age—after clicking “I Agree” 19 times and proving they can identify all squares containing a forklift. Why make it painful for Java? Security through obscurity (mostly obscurity). KPI-driven gatekeeping (“Look, weekly active logins doubled!”). Untouchable Legacy Portal™ with a sacred cron job from 2009. “Roadmap considerations,” i.e., shrug emoji in business casual. So if Python gets a red carpet, could Java at least have a hazmat mat ? Better yet, go feral: ship a Java SDK that actually mirrors pyVmomi, put the docs in the daylight like it’s the current century, and let us get stuff done. We’ll even read them. After [code] , we’ve got days . Why does Python get a red carpet to vSphere while Java gets a CAPTCHA and a shrug?

title: Guideline for method ordering

In particular, I'm interested in which should go first: private methods invoked from a constructor or public methods. One the one hand, it is advised, e.g. in Clean Code, to declare methods right after the first method from which it is first invoked. In general we want function call dependencies to point in the downward direction. That is, a function that is called should be below a function that does the calling. This creates a nice flow down the source code module from high level to low level. Clean Code. Chapter 5, "Formatting". On the other hand, some say public methods should be declared first since one should be able to tell what a class does (not how it does it) at first glance at the source file. If a class is a GUI component, for example, initialization logic may be contained in a big number of private methods (e.g. [code] , [code] ) which would pull any of its public methods way down if the latter have a lower priority. Specifically, for a parameterized type, such as is represented by [code] , a raw type, such as is represented by [code] , should be in the set: Given a generic class or interface C with type parameters F1,…,Fn ( n > 0), the direct supertypes of the parameterized type C<T1,...,Tn>, where each of Ti (1 ≤ i ≤ n ) is a type, are all of the following: The substitution [F1:=T1,...,Fn:=Tn] applied to the direct superclass type of C, if C is a class. The substitution [F1:=T1,...,Fn:=Tn] applied to the direct superinterface types of C. C<S1,...,Sn>, where Si contains Ti (1 ≤ i ≤ n ) ( §4.5.1 ). The type [code] , if C is an interface with no direct superinterface types. The raw type C.
